43012290.text: The generation of human gametes from somatic cells represents a major goal in reproductive medicine, with significant implications for infertility treatment and disease modeling. Among candidate sources, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have emerged as a promising platform due to their multipotency, accessibility, and immunomodulatory properties. Increasing evidence indicates that MSCs can be directed toward germline- and gamete-like phenotypes; however, differentiation efficiency, reproducibility, and functional competence remain major challenges. The present narrative review analyzes current advances in the differentiation of human MSCs into germline- and gametelike phenotypes, integrating findings from 36 studies published between 2000 and 2026. Key chemical and biological drivers, including retinoic acid and bone morphogenetic proteins, are highlighted for their roles in meiotic initiation and primordial germ cell specification. Importantly, germline induction depends on the coordinated interplay of biochemical signals, genetic and epigenetic regulators, and microenvironmental cues. Niche-mimicking strategies, such as co-culture systems, gonadalconditioned media, three-dimensional scaffolds, and in vivo transplantation, enhance differentiation by partially recapitulating the native germline environment. Emerging approaches, including microRNA modulation, gene overexpression, and photobiomodulation, further improve lineage commitment. Despite these advances, most MSC-derived cells remain at early or pre-meiotic stages, with limited evidence of complete meiosis or functional competence. Major barriers to clinical translation include low differentiation efficiency, lack of standardized protocols, incomplete epigenetic reprogramming, and insufficient functional validation. Addressing these challenges will require the development of integrative, stage-specific differentiation systems that better replicate human germline development, advancing the goal of generating functional human gametes in vitro.

20925130.text: The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of a novel bioactive material (Biosilicate®) and low-level laser therapy (LLLT) on bone fracture consolidation in osteoporotic rats. Forty female Wistar rats were submitted to ovariectomy (OVX) to induce osteopenia. Eight weeks after surgery, the animals were randomly divided into four groups of 10 animals each: a bone defect control group (CG); a bone defect filled with Biosilicate group (BG); a bone defect filled with Biosilicate and irradiated with LLLT at 60 J/cm(2) group (BG60); and a bone defect filled with Biosilicate and irradiated with LLLT at 120 J/cm(2) group (BG120). Bone defects were surgically performed on both tibias. The size of particle used for Biosilicate was 180-212 µm. Histopathological analysis showed that bone defects were predominantly filled with the biomaterial in specimens treated with Biosilicate. LLLT with either 60 or 120 J/cm(2) was able to increase collagen, Cbfa-1, VGEF and COX-2 expression in the circumjacent cells of the biomaterial. A morphometric analysis revealed that the Biosilicate + laser groups showed a higher amount of newly formed bone. Our results indicate that laser therapy improves bone repair process in contact with Biosilicate as a result of increasing bone formation, as well as COX-2 and Cbfa-1 immunoexpression, angiogenesis and collagen deposition in osteoporotic rats.
